issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette: Rajiv, a 75-year-old South Asian man, has lived most of his life in the United States after fleeing from the political unrest and violence that plagued his homeland. As a potter by profession, Rajiv found solace and a sense of purpose in crafting intricate pottery designs, but since his traumatic experiences as a refugee, he has struggled to find peace in his daily life. The trauma began during a violent uprising where Rajiv witnessed unspeakable acts of violence that left deep emotional scars. The events are etched in his mind, yet they remain fragmented and difficult to articulate clearly. He recalls vivid images but cannot piece them together coherently. These memories feel more real than any other experiences he has had since arriving in America. Rajiv's triggers include funerals, police presence, and the sound of car horns—sounds that often remind him of the chaos and danger back home. Each time these triggers are encountered, they intensify his sense of vulnerability and fear. For instance, when Rajiv hears a siren while working at his pottery studio, he immediately freezes, scanning the room for any signs of threat. This constant vigilance has left him feeling exhausted and hyper-aware, as if the world around him is always on the brink of collapsing. The memories that haunt Rajiv are more than just painful; they contribute to his maladaptive strategies. He avoids situations where he might feel happy or hopeful, believing these emotions will only be shattered by the memories. Similarly, any potential conflict makes him anxious and uncomfortable, leading him to avoid confrontations at all costs. These avoidance behaviors have seeped into his daily life, affecting both his work as a potter and his relationships with others. Rajiv’s wife has noticed that he no longer takes part in community events or enjoys the company of friends, which has strained their relationship. Even simple activities like driving to the market can become overwhelming due to the constant fear of encountering police officers or hearing car horns. These triggers have reinforced Rajiv's belief that he is no longer capable of handling life’s challenges and that he cannot cope with even minor disturbances. The negative appraisals have created a vicious cycle for Rajiv, where his beliefs about himself and his surroundings perpetuate the very triggers he seeks to avoid. For instance, when he encounters a funeral procession on the way back from buying clay, the fragmented memories of his homeland’s violence surge to the surface, leaving him feeling utterly helpless and reinforcing his belief that he is not capable of navigating life's challenges. Rajiv has begun to feel increasingly isolated as these avoidance strategies have taken hold. He avoids social gatherings and even family events where there might be a risk of confrontation or encountering police officers. His constant vigilance and fear have also made it difficult for him to focus on his pottery, which once brought him joy and a sense of identity. It is this loss that has finally prompted Rajiv to seek help. He had come to believe that he was no longer the capable potter he once was, and this self-perception has led to a profound sense of helplessness. What frightens him most is the idea of losing his ability to create pottery, which he sees as the last vestige of his former life. Rajiv hopes for a way to reclaim some semblance of normalcy and peace in his life, free from the haunting memories that have taken such a toll on his well-being.
